name: net use - Windows Null Session IPC$
description: Establishes a null session to the IPC$ share on a Windows domain controller from a Windows host. Enables anonymous enumeration of domain info via RPC. Rarely works on modern patched Windows (anonymous sessions disabled by default) but still found in legacy environments and can be used as a prerequisite for other net commands.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY IPC$ NULL SESSION ===
IPC$ (Inter-Process Communication) is a special share that enables RPC connections.
A null session to IPC$ with empty username/password allows anonymous RPC calls
if the DC permits it (RestrictAnonymous = 0 in registry).

=== WHEN IT WORKS ===
  Windows NT/2000       → always works by default
  Windows 2003+         → restricted by default, RestrictAnonymous GPO
  Windows 2008+/modern  → almost always blocked
  Lab environments      → often enabled for learning

=== AFTER ESTABLISHING NULL SESSION ===
  net view \\<dc>       → list shares
  net user /domain      → list domain users (if allowed)
  net group /domain     → list domain groups
  nbtstat -A <ip>       → NetBIOS names

=== CHECK IF IT WORKED ===
net use output:
  'The command completed successfully.' = null session established
  'System error 5' = access denied
  'System error 1326' = bad password/account

=== CLEAN UP ===
net use \\<dc>\ipc$ /delete  → remove the connection

examples.label: List domain users after null session

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: Establishes an anonymous/null SMB session (net use \\dc\ipc$ "" /u:"") to enable unauthenticated enumeration where it is permitted.
defense.prerequisites: Domain credentials or null/guest access and SMB (445) reachable.
defense.impact: A null-session foothold for RPC/SAMR enumeration.
defense.detection: SMB tree-connects and share/RID enumeration (Event 5140/5145 with share auditing); anonymous/null binds and RID cycling against the DC.
defense.artifacts: An anonymous IPC$ connection; subsequent RPC queries.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: SMB null sessions are allowed — the server accepts anonymous (unauthenticated) IPC$ connections, exposing share lists, user lists, password policy, and domain information. On older Windows versions (pre-2008 R2) this was the default. On modern systems it can be re-enabled by misconfiguration or GPO rollback. Additionally, SMB signing may be disabled, enabling relay attacks.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Windows Registry — null sessions enabled:
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters
#   RestrictAnonymous = 0      <-- allows null session enumeration
#   RestrictAnonymousSAM = 0   <-- exposes SAM account list anonymously

# SMB signing disabled (relay attack enabler):
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters
#   RequireSecuritySignature = 0
#   EnableSecuritySignature  = 0

# Verify current state:
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMBQUIC,RequireSecuritySignature
defense.secure_config:
# Disable null sessions:
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' \
    -Name RestrictAnonymous -Value 2
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' \
    -Name RestrictAnonymous -Value 1

# Enable SMB signing (blocks NTLM relay attacks):
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force
Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force

# GPO path:
# Computer Config > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options:
#   'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled
#   'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts' = Enabled
#   'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' = Enabled
